## Pre-existing issues found during code review of PR #6267

These were identified by Augment Code during review of the cmd_gaps() refactor (PR #6267). They are pre-existing and were not introduced by that PR.

### Finding 1 — `--status` flag unused in `cmd_list` (low)

`--status` is parsed into `status_filter` but never applied to `where_clause`/`query`. Running `list --status published` has no effect. Either wire it into the SQL filter or remove the flag.

File: `.agents/scripts/content-calendar-helper.sh` ~line 205

### Finding 2 — Missing SQL escaping in `cmd_add` (medium)

Only `title`/`pillar`/`cluster`/`notes` are SQL-escaped. `intent`, `author`, and `tags` are interpolated directly into the INSERT. An author name with an apostrophe will break the query.

File: `.agents/scripts/content-calendar-helper.sh` ~line 187

### Finding 3 — Unvalidated numeric IDs in SQL queries (medium)

`content_id`/`item_id` are interpolated unquoted into SQL (`WHERE id = ${content_id}`). Non-numeric input can cause SQL errors. Validate IDs are strictly numeric before use.

File: `.agents/scripts/content-calendar-helper.sh` lines ~314, 326, 430, 531, 542

### Suggested fix

Add numeric validation helper and escape all string inputs before SQL interpolation.

title: Bug: sandbox-exec-helper.sh fails to enforce --timeout, worker processes persist as zombies
body:
**Observed**: PID 88026 was dispatched via sandbox-exec-helper.sh with --timeout 3600 (1h). The process ran for 18+ hours in SN (sleeping/low-priority) state without being terminated. The sandbox timeout enforcement failed silently.

**Evidence**: 
- Process state: SN (sleeping, low priority) for 18+ hours
- Dispatch command included: --timeout 3600
- Expected: process killed at ~1h mark
- Actual: process persisted until manually killed by pulse supervisor

**Root cause hypothesis**: The sandbox-exec-helper.sh timeout mechanism (likely using `timeout` command or a background kill) may not handle processes that enter a sleep/low-priority state correctly. The `timeout` command on macOS may not propagate SIGTERM to child processes in SN state.

**Impact**: Zombie worker processes consume no CPU but hold open file handles, worktree locks, and appear as 'active' in pulse worker counts if not using process-state filtering. In this case the pulse-state snapshot showed struggle_ratio: 40 (40msgs/0commits) suggesting the process had been stuck for a long time.

**Proposed fix**: Add a secondary watchdog in sandbox-exec-helper.sh that uses `kill -0 PID` polling + wall-clock elapsed check, independent of the `timeout` command. Also add process state filtering in list_active_worker_processes to exclude SN/zombie processes.

title: Bug: pulse dispatches workers for duplicate issues when feature already merged
body:
## Observed behaviour

The pulse created 6 duplicate issues for the same feature (universal tax fallback) on the same day:
- #426, #437, #455, #460, #465, #468 — all describing the same task

PR #456 merged and closed #455. The pulse then dispatched a worker against #468 (still OPEN, status:queued). The worker correctly detected the work was done and closed the issue — but only after being dispatched unnecessarily.

## Root cause

Two gaps:

**Gap 1 — No deduplication at issue creation time.** Before `gh issue create`, there is no check for existing issues with similar titles. If issue-sync runs multiple times (or multiple workers each create their own issue), duplicates accumulate.

**Gap 2 — Dispatch checks OPEN state but not related merged PRs.** The pulse correctly skips CLOSED issues. But it does not check whether a merged PR already implements the same feature. A duplicate issue that was never linked to the merged PR stays OPEN and gets dispatched.

## Proposed fixes

1. **Issue creation dedup**: before `gh issue create` in issue-sync-helper.sh and claim-task-id.sh, run `gh issue list --search "<title keywords>" --state all` and skip creation if a semantically similar issue exists (open or recently closed).

2. **Pre-dispatch merged-PR check**: in the pulse dispatch step, before assigning a worker, search for merged PRs that reference the issue's task keywords. If found, close the duplicate issue with a comment pointing to the merged PR instead of dispatching.

3. **Single-issue-per-task enforcement**: claim-task-id.sh should store the GH issue number atomically alongside the task ID claim, preventing a second claim from creating a second issue for the same task ID.

## Evidence

- Issues: #426, #437, #455, #460, #465, #468 (Ultimate-Multisite/ultimate-multisite) — all same feature, same day
- Merged PR: #456 (closed #455 only)
- Wasted dispatch: worker on #468 spent time verifying work already done

🌐 Web query:

`head -n -1 portability BSD macOS GNU coreutils negative line count`

💡 Result:

The head -n -1 command, intended to print all lines except the last one, is not portable across BSD/macOS and GNU coreutils implementations. GNU coreutils head (common on Linux) supports -n -num to print all except the last num lines. Official docs confirm: "-n [-]num: Output the first num lines. On macOS as of 2026-03-25, native head -n -1 fails. Workarounds: - Install GNU coreutils via Homebrew (brew install coreutils), use ghead -n -1. - Portable alternatives: sed '$d' (delete last line), head -n $(( $(wc -l < file) - 1 )) file. title: Bug: headless-runtime-helper.sh spawns 2 processes per dispatch (duplicate sandbox-exec + opencode)
body:
Observed in pulse session 2026-03-25: each dispatch via headless-runtime-helper.sh creates 2 headless-runtime-helper.sh processes and 2 sandbox-exec-helper.sh processes for the same session-key. Seen for issues #6426, #6427, #6428, #6429, #6430 — consistently 2 PIDs per issue.

Root cause hypothesis: headless-runtime-helper.sh is being called twice per dispatch — likely the pulse wrapper's backfill cycle re-dispatches issues that were already dispatched in the LLM pass, because check_worker_launch returns false-negative (processes exist but validation fails).

Evidence: ps shows 2x headless-runtime-helper.sh + 2x sandbox-exec-helper.sh per session-key. check_worker_launch returns INVALID even when processes are running.

Impact: doubles compute cost per task, causes struggle_ratio inflation (2 workers competing on same worktree), and may cause branch conflicts.

Proposed fix: (1) Fix check_worker_launch to correctly detect running processes by session-key. (2) Add session-key dedup guard in pulse-wrapper.sh backfill cycle to skip issues already dispatched in the LLM pass.

🌐 Web query:

`head -n -1 portability BSD macOS GNU coreutils negative line count`

💡 Result:

The head -n -1 command, intended to print all lines except the last one, is not portable across BSD/macOS and GNU coreutils implementations. GNU coreutils head (common on Linux) supports -n -num to print all except the last num lines. Official docs confirm: "-n [-]num: Output the first num lines. However, if num is prefixed with a '-', print all but the last num lines of each file." macOS (BSD-derived) and other BSDs (FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD) head do not support negative counts for -n; they require positive decimal integers and error with "head: illegal line count -- -1". macOS man page: "-n count: Print count lines..."; POSIX spec: "The application shall ensure that the number option-argument is a positive decimal integer." On macOS as of 2026-03-25, native head -n -1 fails. Workarounds: - Install GNU coreutils via Homebrew (brew install coreutils), use ghead -n -1. - Portable alternatives: sed '$d' (delete last line), head -n $(( $(wc -l < file) - 1 )) file. Sources confirm consistent behavior in man pages and Stack Overflow reports from 2013-2023.

title: Research: redesign worktree auto-cleanup to prevent deletion of active work
body:
## Problem

Pulse auto-cleanup (`worktree-helper.sh clean --auto --force-merged`) deletes worktrees with committed in-progress work. Even making a WIP commit does not protect the worktree — it was explicitly reported that a worktree in another project was deleted despite a deliberate WIP commit.

### Root cause

The cleanup logic is **inverted**: it deletes by default and tries to guess what to keep. The "is merged" detection has multiple paths that produce false positives for active work:

**Check 1: `git branch --merged`** — A branch merged into default (e.g., via PR to main/staging) is flagged. But merged != done — the developer may still need the worktree for follow-up work.

**Check 2: "remote deleted"** — If `git fetch --prune` removes the remote ref (GitHub auto-delete after PR merge, or manual remote branch deletion), the worktree is flagged. A pushed WIP branch whose remote is deleted is treated as abandoned.

**Check 3: "squash-merged PR"** — `gh pr list --state merged` matches the branch. Again, merged PR != done working.

### Why existing safety checks (GH#5694) don't help

| Safety check | What it protects | What it misses |
|---|---|---|
| Grace period (< 4h) | Fresh worktrees | Work older than 4 hours |
| Open PR | Worktrees with open PRs | Work without PR, or PR already merged |
| Zero-commit + dirty | Freshly created, uncommitted | Any committed work (1+ commits = not zero) |
| Dirty check | Uncommitted files (without --force-merged) | Clean worktrees (everything committed) |
| Ownership (PID alive) | Active sessions | Sessions that ended (PID dead) |

**Key gap**: once you commit your work, the worktree becomes "clean" — removing the only remaining barrier. `--force-merged` (always passed by pulse) overrides the dirty check anyway.

### Attack scenario (confirmed by user)

1. Create worktree, work on feature
2. Make WIP commit to protect work (deliberate defensive action)
3. Push to remote, maybe create PR
4. PR gets merged (or remote branch deleted for any reason)
5. Pulse runs cleanup (every 2 min)
6. `git branch --merged` or "remote deleted" → `is_merged=true`
7. Worktree is clean (WIP committed) → dirty check passes
8. Grace period passed (>4h) → grace check passes
9. **Worktree deleted with all local work**

Git objects survive in the reflog temporarily, but the worktree directory and local branch ref are gone.

## Design options to evaluate

### A. Disable auto-cleanup entirely
Pulse doesn't touch worktrees. Manual cleanup via `worktree-helper.sh clean` (interactive, with confirmation). Zero code, zero risk. Worktrees are cheap (shared .git).

### B. Lock file (.worktree-keep)
`worktree-helper.sh add` creates `.worktree-keep` automatically. Cleanup always skips worktrees with this file. Removed explicitly via `worktree-helper.sh done <branch>`. Workers call `done` after successful PR merge.

### C. Soft delete (archive)
Instead of `rm -rf`, move to `~/Git/.archive/`. Auto-purge archive after 30 days. Always recoverable.

### D. Separate bot/human worktrees
Mark worktrees at creation with creator type (headless worker vs interactive session). Auto-cleanup ONLY for bot-created worktrees. Human worktrees are never auto-cleaned.

### E. Age-based only (30+ days)
Remove worktrees older than N days regardless of merge status. Simple, predictable. Risk: long-lived feature branches.

### F. Two-phase (mark → wait 24-48h → delete)
Pulse creates `.worktree-pending-removal`. After 24-48h, if not cancelled by user, actually deletes. Gives a window to intervene.

### G. Combination D + C
Bot worktrees → soft delete to archive. Human worktrees → never auto-clean.

## Evaluation criteria

- Safety: probability of data loss under normal use
- Simplicity: lines of code, moving parts, potential for new bugs
- User friction: manual steps required
- Disk usage: worktree accumulation impact
- Compatibility: works with current pulse/worker lifecycle

## Recommendation (preliminary)

**Option A (disable auto-cleanup)** is the safest starting point. Worktrees are lightweight (shared .git object store), 50 worktrees ≠ 50 repo clones. Interactive `worktree-helper.sh clean` already exists for manual cleanup. Zero new code = zero new bugs.

If accumulation becomes a real problem, layer **D (bot/human separation)** on top.

## References

- GH#5694: initial safety checks (grace period, open PR, zero-commit)
- Memory: `mem_20260325044328_89f5f7eb` — original incident report
- `pulse-wrapper.sh:2065` — caller with `--force-merged`
- `worktree-helper.sh:1035-1084` — `_clean_classify_worktree()`
- `worktree-helper.sh:927-994` — `should_skip_cleanup()`

title: Research: Patterns from obra/superpowers — reassessed for convolution/fragility risk
body:
## Context

Analysis of [obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) v5.0.6 — a composable skills plugin for Claude Code/Cursor/Codex/Gemini that enforces structured dev workflows via prompt engineering. 15+ skills, battle-tested through what they call "TDD for documentation" (baseline-test agent failures, write counters, re-test).

Full analysis: [mainframe/todo/superpowers-gap-analysis.md](https://github.com/johnwaldo/mainframe/blob/main/todo/superpowers-gap-analysis.md)

## Reassessment: Convolution & Fragility Filter

Superpowers ships to strangers who install it cold — no framework, no supervisor, no session history. It **needs** rigid gates because there's nothing else. aidevops already has intelligent orchestration, session memory, pre-edit checks, review-bot gates, and the "Intelligence Over Determinism" principle. Adding rigid mechanisms on top risks:

- **Convolution**: More rules = more context tokens = less room for actual work. Overlapping rules create confusion about precedence.
- **Fragility**: Hard gates break on edge cases. A "must have brief before code" gate blocks a 2-line hotfix. A "banned words" list catches legitimate hedging. A two-stage review loop triples dispatch cost for trivial tasks.

Each of the 8 original gaps is reassessed below into one of three buckets:

### Adopt as Guidance (sharpens judgment, no new mechanism)

**Gap 4: Three-fix escalation heuristic** — One sentence in build.txt: "If 3+ fix attempts each reveal a new problem in a different location, stop and question the architecture." This is pure guidance. No gate, no state tracking, no mechanism. The agent already has judgment — this gives it a named pattern to recognise. **Recommend adopting.**

**Gap 8: CSO — skill descriptions should be triggers, not summaries** — Superpowers found that descriptions summarising workflow caused Claude to follow the summary instead of reading the full skill. Fix: descriptions say "Use when..." (triggering conditions only). This is an audit of existing text, not a new mechanism. Applies to subagent-index.toon and AGENTS.md descriptions. **Recommend adopting.**

**Gap 3: Anti-rationalization awareness** — The research is solid (Meincke et al. 2025, N=28,000, compliance 33%→72%). But the proposed "baseline testing methodology" is heavy process. The lightweight version: when session mining surfaces repeated agent rationalizations for rule violations, add the specific excuse/reality pair to the relevant build.txt section. This is already how build.txt evolves (the error prevention section grew from session mining). No new process needed — just awareness that rationalization tables are a proven format. **Recommend as awareness, not process.**

### Adopt Selectively (valuable in context, harmful if universal)

**Gap 1: Spec compliance check before PR** — Valuable for complex tasks where over/under-building is a real risk. Harmful as a universal gate — it triples cost for trivial tasks and adds a dispatch round-trip. The right approach: make this a judgment call in the worker lifecycle doc. "For tasks with detailed specs/briefs, verify implementation matches spec before creating PR. For straightforward tasks, self-review is sufficient." This aligns with Intelligence Over Determinism. **Recommend as guidance, not gate.**

**Gap 2: Structured status vocabulary** — `DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | NEEDS_CONTEXT | BLOCKED` is useful vocabulary for the supervisor to understand worker outcomes. But making it a rigid protocol (workers MUST report one of four statuses) adds fragility — what about partial completion? What about "done but CI is failing for unrelated reasons"? Better approach: document these as recognised patterns the supervisor should look for, not as a protocol workers must emit. The supervisor already uses judgment to assess PR state, issue comments, and branch activity. **Recommend as vocabulary, not protocol.**

**Gap 7: Plan step granularity for cheap model tiers** — Tier-specific: more granular plans for haiku/flash dispatch, standard briefs for sonnet/opus. This is already implicit in the bundle/tier system. Worth a one-line note in the task taxonomy doc: "For simple-tier tasks, include explicit verification steps — cheaper models skip implicit steps." **Recommend as a note, not a standard.**

### Skip (convolution/fragility outweighs value)

**Gap 5: Verification gate with banned-language list** — aidevops already has "Drive to verified completion" and "Claim discipline (turn-end gate)" in build.txt. The Superpowers version adds a banned-words list ("should", "probably", "seems to") and a rigid gate function. Problem: these words have legitimate uses. "This should work based on the test output" after running tests is fine. "This should work" without running tests is not. The difference is judgment, not vocabulary. Consolidating the existing verification rules is fine, but a banned-language list adds fragility. **Skip the mechanism, keep the principle.**

**Gap 6: Design-before-code hard gate** — Superpowers gates ALL implementation behind design approval, including "a todo list, a single-function utility, a config change." This is appropriate for their context (cold-start plugin, no framework). In aidevops, task briefs are already mandatory and `/full-loop` includes the brief step. Adding a hard gate that blocks a 2-line config fix until a design doc exists is pure convolution. The existing convention + worker judgment is the right level. **Skip.**

## Summary

| Gap | Verdict | Action |
|-----|---------|--------|
| 4. Three-fix escalation | **Adopt** | One sentence in build.txt |
| 8. CSO descriptions | **Adopt** | Audit subagent descriptions |
| 3. Anti-rationalization | **Adopt as awareness** | Use rationalization table format when session mining surfaces patterns |
| 1. Spec compliance check | **Selective** | Guidance for complex tasks, not universal gate |
| 2. Status vocabulary | **Selective** | Document as patterns, not protocol |
| 7. Plan granularity | **Selective** | One-line note in task taxonomy |
| 5. Verification gate | **Skip mechanism** | Existing rules sufficient, banned-words list is fragile |
| 6. Design hard gate | **Skip** | Existing brief convention is the right level |

## Net Recommendation

Three lightweight additions to existing docs (gaps 4, 8, 3). Three awareness notes in existing docs (gaps 1, 2, 7). Zero new mechanisms, zero new gates, zero new scripts. The value from Superpowers is in their research and pattern names, not in their enforcement machinery — aidevops's intelligence-first approach is the right architecture for a framework that manages its own repos.

title: feat: pulse_hours and pulse_expires support in repos.json
body:
## Summary

The pulse wrapper (`pulse-wrapper.sh`) currently only reads `pulse: true/false` from repos.json. Two new fields would enable time-bounded and expiring pulse schedules per repo without launchd changes.

## Proposed Fields

```json
{
  "path": "~/Git/aidevops",
  "slug": "marcusquinn/aidevops",
  "pulse": true,
  "pulse_hours": { "start": 17, "end": 5 },
  "pulse_expires": "2026-03-28"
}
```

### `pulse_hours` (optional)
- `start`/`end` in 24h local time
- Overnight windows supported (e.g., 17→5 wraps across midnight)
- Repos without this field run 24/7 (current behaviour preserved)
- When current hour is outside the window, pulse skips the repo

### `pulse_expires` (optional)
- ISO date string (YYYY-MM-DD)
- When today > expiry date, pulse auto-sets `pulse: false` in repos.json and skips the repo
- One-time cleanup — once disabled, the field is inert

## Motivation

- Run aidevops pulse only during off-hours (17:00–05:00) to avoid conflicts with Marcus's simplification routine during the day
- Temporarily enable pulse on repos with an automatic shutoff date (e.g., "help clear the backlog this week")
- Both fields are optional and backward-compatible — no change to existing repos

## Implementation

~15-20 lines in `pulse-wrapper.sh`:
1. After reading `pulse: true`, check `pulse_expires` — if past, set `pulse: false` via jq and skip
2. Check `pulse_hours` — if current hour outside window, skip
3. Both checks are per-repo in the existing repo iteration loop

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Repos with `pulse_hours` are skipped outside their time window
- [ ] Overnight windows (start > end, e.g., 17→5) work correctly
- [ ] Repos with `pulse_expires` past today are auto-disabled (`pulse` set to `false`)
- [ ] Repos without either field behave exactly as today (24/7, no expiry)
- [ ] Bash 3.2 compatible (no associative arrays, no bash 4+ features)

title: Bug: headless-runtime-helper.sh spawns duplicate worker processes per dispatch call
body:
## Observed

During pulse 2026-03-26T03:00Z, every `headless-runtime-helper.sh run` call spawned TWO sandbox-exec-helper.sh processes with identical arguments. This happened for:
- Issue #6528 (PIDs 4178725 + 4178760)
- Issue #6532 (PIDs 4179366 + 4179410)
- Previously observed for PR #1933 CI fix (PIDs 3474155 + 3474252)

All duplicate pairs had identical command lines, same `--dir`, same `--title`, same `--prompt`.

## Root cause hypothesis

The `headless-runtime-helper.sh run` function likely forks or backgrounds the sandbox-exec-helper.sh call internally, AND the pulse also backgrounds it with `&`. This double-backgrounding creates two processes. Alternatively, the helper may have a retry-on-startup mechanism that fires before the first process is detectable.

## Impact

- Wastes 50% of worker capacity (each dispatch consumes 2 slots instead of 1)
- Duplicate workers race on the same branch, causing git conflicts
- Struggle ratios appear inflated because two workers share the same commit count

## Proposed fix

1. Ensure `headless-runtime-helper.sh run` does NOT background internally when called with `&` from the pulse
2. Or add a PID-file lock so the second spawn detects the first and exits
3. The pulse's `check_worker_launch` validation should detect duplicate PIDs for the same session-key

title: Bug: maintainer-gate retrigger job sets pending commit status but never resolves it
body:
## Observed

PR #6526 and PR #6531 both had `maintainer-gate` commit status stuck at `pending` with description "Re-evaluating after issue #NNNN label change". The linked issues had valid assignees and no `needs-maintainer-review` label, but the status never resolved to success.

## Root cause

In `.github/workflows/maintainer-gate.yml`, the `retrigger` job (triggered by `issues: [labeled, unlabeled]`) posts a `pending` commit status on linked PRs but does NOT trigger a new `pull_request_target` event. The `check-pr` job only runs on `pull_request_target` events (opened, synchronize, reopened, edited). So the pending status is never resolved by a subsequent check-pr run.

The retrigger job correctly identifies linked PRs and posts the pending status, but there's no mechanism to then evaluate the gate and post success/failure.

## Impact

- PRs appear to have failing/pending checks when they should pass
- Requires manual intervention (posting success status via API) or a new commit to trigger re-evaluation
- Blocks auto-merge workflows

## Proposed fix

Option A: Have the retrigger job also evaluate the gate conditions (check assignee + labels on linked issues) and post the final status (success/failure) directly, instead of just posting pending.

Option B: Use `repository_dispatch` or `workflow_dispatch` to trigger a new check-pr run for the affected PRs.

Option A is simpler and more reliable.

title: Bug: OpenAI pool add flow uses callback URL flow, fails with Codex device auth
body:
## Summary
`aidevops model-accounts-pool add openai` currently builds an authorize URL with redirect `http://localhost:1455/auth/callback` and then prompts users to paste an authorization code manually.

In current OpenCode OpenAI login flows, the working path is device auth (`https://auth.openai.com/codex/device`) with a device code and polling, not callback URL copy/paste. Users can complete consent but the pool helper fails on the last step because no pasteable callback code is surfaced.

## Evidence
- `oauth-pool-helper.sh` constants and flow:
  - `OPENAI_AUTHORIZE_URL=https://auth.openai.com/oauth/authorize`
  - `OPENAI_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:1455/auth/callback`
  - prompt: `Paste the authorization code here`
- OpenCode native login method output shows:
  - `Go to: https://auth.openai.com/codex/device`
  - `Enter code: ...`
  - `Waiting for authorization`

## Expected
OpenAI pool add should use a supported login flow that reliably returns tokens for Codex accounts (device auth preferred), without requiring callback URL scraping by the user.

## Proposed fixes
1. Add OpenAI headless/device auth path to `oauth-pool-helper.sh add openai` (poll token endpoint until authorized).
2. Keep callback flow only as fallback behind a flag.
3. Improve UX: accept full callback URL and parse `code` automatically when callback mode is used.
4. Add integration test for OpenAI add flow to prevent regressions.

title: Bug: full-loop task lifecycle is not repo-agnostic when .task-counter is missing
body:
## Description

In project repos using aidevops workflows, full-loop/task allocation is not reliably repo-agnostic when .task-counter is missing.

Observed behavior:
- claim-task-id.sh fails when .task-counter is absent or invalid
- offline fallback also fails if no local .task-counter exists
- implementation/PR flow may still continue, but robust task registration/allocation is broken

This creates inconsistent behavior across repos and weakens traceability for unplanned follow-up work.

## Why this matters

- Breaks deterministic task allocation in some initialized repos
- Increases risk of skipped task registration or ad-hoc ID handling
- Creates inconsistent operator experience across repos
- Undermines the "full-loop is portable across repos" expectation

## Reproduction

1. Use a repo with TODO/task workflows but no .task-counter file.
2. Run claim-task-id.sh with a new title.
3. Observe failure due to missing/invalid .task-counter, including offline fallback failure.
4. Run /full-loop for follow-up work; code/PR may progress, but atomic task allocation path is unavailable.

## Root-cause hypothesis

Two gaps combine:
1. Init-time gap: aidevops init does not always guarantee .task-counter is created/seeded.
2. Runtime resilience gap: claim-task-id/full-loop paths do not auto-bootstrap .task-counter when missing.

## Proposed holistic fix

### 1) Init-time guarantee
- Ensure aidevops init always creates/seeds .task-counter.
- Seed precedence:
  1. Highest task ID found in TODO.md
  2. Otherwise 1
- Include this in auditable planning/bootstrap commit.

### 2) Runtime auto-bootstrap
- In claim-task-id.sh, auto-bootstrap when .task-counter is missing:
  - fetch counter branch
  - compute seed from TODO.md (with safe local/remote fallback)
  - initialize .task-counter via CAS push
- Preserve existing CAS retry behavior for concurrent claims.

### 3) Full-loop resilience
- In /full-loop Step 0 claim/allocation path, detect missing counter and invoke bootstrap automatically.
- Emit explicit machine-readable status markers for observability (e.g., BOOTSTRAP_COUNTER_OK / BOOTSTRAP_COUNTER_FAILED).
- Fail clearly instead of silently bypassing task registration.

### 4) Scenario matrix coverage
Validate for:
- existing .task-counter
- TODO exists but no .task-counter
- fresh repo (no TODO, no counter)
- offline mode
- local_only repos (no GH remote)
- branch protection / push rejection
- concurrent multi-session allocation race

### 5) Documentation and repair UX
- Document counter requirements and auto-bootstrap semantics.
- Add troubleshooting for missing/corrupt counter state.
- Add a non-destructive repair command/path for counter recovery.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] aidevops init leaves repos in a state where first claim-task-id succeeds
- [ ] claim-task-id succeeds with safe auto-bootstrap when counter is missing
- [ ] full-loop can register follow-up tasks without manual counter setup
- [ ] no duplicate task IDs under concurrent claims (CAS preserved)
- [ ] offline behavior is explicit and recoverable
- [ ] automated tests cover bootstrap + concurrency + failure modes
- [ ] docs updated with behavior and recovery guidance

## Related areas

- claim-task-id.sh allocation/bootstrap path
- /full-loop Step 0 task claim/allocation logic
- aidevops init bootstrap invariants
- cross-repo traceability guarantees

title: Bug: quality-debt issues auto-created without assignee block maintainer gate on fix PRs
body:
## Observed Pattern

Quality-debt issues (#6557, #6558, #6559, #6567) are auto-created by the quality sweep without an assignee. When a worker creates a fix PR that links to these issues (via `Closes #NNN`), the Maintainer Review & Assignee Gate blocks the PR because the linked issue has no assignee.

This creates a deadlock: the fix PR can't merge until the issue has an assignee, but the issue was auto-created and no one assigned it.

**Affected PRs this cycle:** #6618, #6619, #6621, #6622 (all blocked by this pattern)
**Systemic cluster:** 9 failed gate events, 3+ in same cluster

## Root Cause

The quality-sweep script (or issue-sync) creates quality-debt issues without setting an assignee. The maintainer gate requires linked issues to have an assignee before a PR can merge.

## Fix Options

1. **Quality sweep auto-assigns to repo owner** when creating quality-debt issues — simplest fix
2. **Maintainer gate exempts quality-debt label** — issues with `quality-debt` label bypass the assignee check
3. **Quality sweep adds `auto-dispatch` label** — pulse auto-assigns when dispatching a worker

Option 2 is lowest risk: quality-debt issues are auto-generated by trusted tooling, not external contributors, so the assignee gate adds no security value for them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Fix PRs for quality-debt issues are not blocked by the maintainer gate
- [ ] Existing blocked PRs (#6618, #6619, #6621, #6622) can merge after fix
- [ ] No regression: external contributor PRs still require the gate

title: Bug: tool-version-check.sh reports Crawl4AI as "not installed" when it is installed as pip package
body:
### Description

tool-version-check.sh reports Crawl4AI as "not installed" even though it is installed (v0.8.6 via pip).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install Crawl4AI: `pip install crawl4ai`
2. Run `aidevops update` or tool version check
3. Output shows: `○  Crawl4AI: not installed`

### Expected Behavior

Should detect Crawl4AI as installed (v0.8.6) and show it as up-to-date.

### Error Output

The detection entry in PIP_TOOLS (line 108):

```
"pip|Crawl4AI|crawl4ai|--version|crawl4ai|pip install --upgrade crawl4ai"
```

uses `command -v crawl4ai` but Crawl4AI is a Python library with no CLI binary. `command -v crawl4ai` returns "command not found", while `python3 -c "from crawl4ai.__version__ import __version__; print(__version__)"` returns "0.8.6".

The `get_installed_version()` function only checks `command -v` (line 157). pip-only libraries need a python-import-based detection path.

### Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.271
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **gh CLI**: gh version 2.88.1

title: Bug: generate-runtime-config.sh subagent generation fails — $agent_dir not exported to xargs subshells
body:
### Description

`_generate_subagents_opencode()` in `generate-runtime-config.sh` fails to generate any subagent stubs. All ~2,837 writes fail with `environment: /<name>.md: Permission denied`. The `~/.config/opencode/agent/` directory is left empty.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `aidevops update` on Linux (bash 5.x)
2. Observe hundreds of `environment: /SKILL.md: Permission denied` during "Generating subagent markdown files..."
3. Check: `ls ~/.config/opencode/agent/` → empty

### Expected Behavior

~2,837 subagent markdown stubs should be generated in `~/.config/opencode/agent/`.

### Error Output

```shell
[INFO] Generating subagent markdown files...
environment: /revenuecat.md: Permission denied
environment: /SKILL.md: Permission denied
environment: /procurement.md: Permission denied
# ... hundreds more ...
```

### Root Cause

`generate-runtime-config.sh` lines 738–841:

- **Line 739**: `local agent_dir="$1"` — local to `_generate_subagents_opencode()`
- **Lines 748–827**: nested function `generate_subagent_stub()` references `$agent_dir` on line 825
- **Line 829**: `export -f generate_subagent_stub` — exports function for xargs
- **Line 830**: `export AGENTS_DIR` — exports `AGENTS_DIR` but **NOT** `agent_dir`
- **Line 837**: `xargs -0 -P ... bash -c 'generate_subagent_stub "$@"'` — spawns subshells

In the xargs subshells, `$agent_dir` is undefined (empty). The redirect on line 825 `>"$agent_dir/$name.md"` becomes `>"/$name.md"` — attempting to write to root filesystem.

The `environment:` prefix is bash 5.x behavior: errors from functions imported via `export -f` are labeled `environment:` instead of `bash:`.

**Standalone reproduction:**

```shell
bash -c '
f() {
  local d="/tmp/test"
  g() { { echo x; } >"$d/out.md"; }
  export -f g
  echo x | xargs -I{} bash -c "g" 2>&1
}
f'
# Output: environment: /out.md: Permission denied
```

### Suggested Fix

Add `export agent_dir` on line 830 alongside `export AGENTS_DIR`. `local` and `export` coexist in bash — confirmed by testing that the value propagates to xargs subshells correctly.

### Impact

- **0 / ~2,837** subagent stubs generated
- All `@subagent` routing in OpenCode broken (domain-specific agents like `@wordpress`, `@dataforseo`, `@accessibility-audit`, etc.)
- Primary agents (14, defined in `opencode.json`) unaffected
- Task tool subagent types (MCP-sourced) unaffected
- Likely affects all Linux / bash 5.x users; may also affect macOS if using homebrew bash 5.x

### Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.271
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **gh CLI**: gh version 2.88.1

title: Bug: pulse dispatch loop creates duplicate workers for same target — no in-flight tracking
body:
## Summary

When the supervisor pulse dispatches workers in a continuous loop (e.g., simplification batch), it re-dispatches the same target file multiple times because there's no tracking of in-flight workers between dispatch and PR creation. This wastes tokens, creates conflicting worktrees, and produces duplicate or failed PRs.

## Observed Behavior (2026-03-26, interactive session)

### Timeline

1. **16:02 UTC** — Autonomous pulse script launched to simplify `.agents/*.md` files >15KB. 6 worker slots, 2-minute poll interval.
2. **16:02–16:18 UTC** — Pulse ran 8 cycles. `CHAPTER-12.md` was dispatched **4 times** because:
   - Workers take 10-15min to create a worktree, simplify, push, and open a PR
   - During that window, the file has no open PR on GitHub
   - The pulse's dedup check (`gh pr list --state open`) finds nothing → re-dispatches
3. **16:18 UTC** — User noticed only 1 of ~19 dispatches had produced a merged PR. Workers were creating local worktrees but colliding or failing to push.
4. **16:21 UTC** — Killed pulse, wrote v2 with in-memory `DISPATCHED_FILES` tracking. This fixed the immediate problem but is lost on script restart.

### Evidence: duplicate worktrees for the same file

```
/Users/justin/Git/aidevops-chore-simplify-chapter-12    [chore/simplify-chapter-12]
/Users/justin/Git/aidevops-chore-simplify-chapter12     [chore/simplify-chapter12]
/Users/justin/Git/aidevops-chore-simplify-cro-ch12      [chore/simplify-cro-ch12]
```

Three worktrees for the same target file, created by three different workers with slightly different branch names. 47 total simplification worktrees accumulated during the session.

### Evidence: unreliable worker counting

`pgrep -f '/full-loop'` reported 24 matches when only 6 workers were running — parent processes (sandbox-exec-helper, headless-runtime-helper) also match the pattern, inflating the count. This caused the pulse to believe slots were full when they weren't, and vice versa.

## Root Causes

### A. No in-flight dispatch tracking (primary)
The pulse checks GitHub for open PRs to detect "already handled" targets. But workers take 10-15 minutes between dispatch and PR creation. During this window, the target appears unhandled and gets re-dispatched every 2-minute cycle.

### B. Non-deterministic worktree naming
`/full-loop` generates branch/worktree names from the task description. Different prompt phrasings for the same file produce different branch names (`chore/simplify-chapter-12` vs `chore/simplify-cro-ch12`), so git doesn't prevent the collision.

### C. Unreliable worker process counting
`pgrep -f '/full-loop'` matches parent wrapper processes (sandbox-exec-helper, headless-runtime-helper), not just the actual opencode worker. This inflates the count by 2-4x.

### D. No file-level lock
Multiple workers can create worktrees targeting the same file simultaneously. There's no mutex or lock file to prevent this.

## Proposed Fix

### Dispatch ledger (lightweight, file-based)
A simple file-based ledger at `~/.aidevops/.agent-workspace/tmp/dispatch-ledger.jsonl` where each dispatch appends a line:

```jsonl
{"target": ".agents/tools/marketing/cro/CHAPTER-12.md", "session_key": "simplify-ch12-1711468800", "dispatched_at": "2026-03-26T16:02:47Z", "status": "in-flight"}
```

The pulse checks this ledger before dispatching. Entries expire after 60 minutes (configurable) or are marked `completed`/`failed` by the worker on exit. This survives script restarts without requiring a database.

### Deterministic branch naming
When dispatching simplification work, the pulse should pass a deterministic branch name derived from the target file path (e.g., `simplify/{basename}-{short-hash}`), not let `/full-loop` generate one from the prompt text.

### Reliable worker counting
Replace `pgrep -f '/full-loop'` with a count of active session keys in the dispatch ledger, or use `pgrep` with a more specific pattern that excludes wrapper processes.

## Impact

- **Token waste**: 4x duplicate dispatches per file × ~$0.50-1.00 per simplification = significant cost at scale across 75+ files
- **Worktree pollution**: 47 orphaned worktrees consuming disk space
- **User friction**: required manual intervention to diagnose and fix mid-session
- **Throughput loss**: ~16 minutes of the session spent debugging instead of simplifying

title: Bug: workers never clean up worktrees after PR merge — accumulation blocks new dispatches
body:
## Summary

Workers created by `/full-loop` create git worktrees but never remove them after the PR is merged (or closed). Over a batch session, worktrees accumulate indefinitely (observed: 110 worktrees) until new workers fail silently — they can't create worktrees or hit filesystem limits.

## Observed Behavior

During a simplification batch session dispatching ~50 workers:

1. Each worker creates a worktree at `~/Git/aidevops-{type}-{name}/`
2. Worker completes, pushes branch, creates PR, exits
3. Worktree directory and git reference remain permanently
4. After ~50 dispatches: 110 worktrees accumulated
5. Final batch of 7 workers all failed silently — 0 of 7 created PRs
6. After manually cleaning 75 orphaned worktrees (110 → 35), redispatched workers succeeded (4 of 7 created PRs)

## Root Cause

The `/full-loop` worker lifecycle has no cleanup phase. The worker exits after PR creation. There is no:
- Post-merge worktree cleanup hook
- Worker exit cleanup step
- Periodic worktree garbage collection
- Worktree count check before creating new ones

## Impact

- **Silent worker failures**: workers fail to create worktrees but don't report the error — they just exit with no PR
- **Disk waste**: each worktree is a full checkout (~50-100MB for aidevops). 110 worktrees = ~5-10GB
- **Blocks batch operations**: any batch dispatch (simplification, quality-debt, etc.) will hit this wall after ~50-80 dispatches
- **Manual intervention required**: user must run `git worktree prune` + `rm -rf` to recover

## Proposed Fix

### Option A: Worker self-cleanup (preferred)
Add a cleanup step to `/full-loop` after PR creation:
```bash
# After PR is created and verified
git worktree remove --force "$WORKTREE_PATH" 2>/dev/null
```

### Option B: Periodic garbage collection
Add a step to the pulse wrapper that prunes merged worktrees:
```bash
# In pulse-wrapper.sh, once per hour
git worktree list | while read path ref branch; do
  # Check if the branch's PR was merged
  # If so, remove the worktree
done
git worktree prune
```

### Option C: Pre-dispatch check
Before creating a worktree, check the count and clean up stale ones:
```bash
WORKTREE_COUNT=$(git worktree list | wc -l)
if [ "$WORKTREE_COUNT" -gt 50 ]; then
  # Prune worktrees for merged PRs before proceeding
fi
```

Recommendation: Option A + C. Workers clean up after themselves, and a safety valve prevents accumulation if cleanup fails.

## Related

- GH#6696 — duplicate dispatch (worktree naming collisions are a symptom of accumulation)
- GH#6704 — zsh IFS bug (discovered while debugging this issue)

title: Bug: claim-task-id.sh outputs unpadded task IDs — mismatches todo-template.md convention
body:
## Summary

`claim-task-id.sh` outputs raw integers (`t44`, `t1`, `t10`) but the `todo-template.md` format section defines zero-padded IDs (`t001`, `t002`, `t003`). Every repo using aidevops has this mismatch.

## Root Cause

`claim-task-id.sh` line 938 (and 5 other output points):
```bash
echo "task_id=t${first_id}"
```

`first_id` is a raw integer from `.task-counter`. No zero-padding is applied.

**Affected output lines**: 547, 593, 828, 938, 940, 941 — all use `t${first_id}` or `t${last_id}` with no formatting.

## Expected Behavior

Output should match `todo-template.md` convention: minimum 3-digit zero-padded (`t001`..`t999`..`t1000`).

```bash
# Current:  echo "task_id=t${first_id}"     → t44
# Expected: printf "task_id=t%03d" "$first_id"  → t044
```

At `t1000+`, `%03d` naturally produces 4 digits (`t1000`) which is fine — the minimum width just ensures consistency for `t001`-`t999`.

## Template Evidence

`~/.aidevops/agents/templates/todo-template.md` lines 14-25:
```markdown
- [ ] t001 Task description @owner #tag ~30m
- [ ] t002 Dependent task blocked-by:t001 ~15m
- [ ] t001.1 Subtask of t001 ~10m
- [x] t003 Completed task ~30m actual:25m

**Task IDs:**
- `t001` - Top-level task
- `t001.1` - Subtask of t001
```

## Reproduction

```bash
# In any repo with .task-counter at a value < 100:
claim-task-id.sh --no-issue --title "test"
# Outputs: task_id=tNN (unpadded)
# Expected: task_id=t0NN (padded)
```

## Discovered In

qs-agency session 2026-03-26. Counter allocated `t44`, existing convention was `t001`-`t043`. Required manual rename to `t044`.

## Scope

All 6 output points in `claim-task-id.sh` need the same fix. The log messages (lines 547, 593, 828) should also use padded format for consistency.

title: bug: tool-version-check.sh fails to update on Linux — hardcoded brew + bare pip blocked by PEP 668
body:
## Description

`tool-version-check.sh` has two platform compatibility bugs that cause silent update failures on Linux:

1. **Brew tools (gh, glab, jq, shellcheck, etc.)**: Update commands are hardcoded to `brew upgrade <pkg>` (line 96-103). On Linux without Homebrew, the version check correctly detects outdated packages (gh falls back to the GitHub API at line 284), but the update silently fails because `brew` doesn't exist. gh is installed via the official apt repository (`/usr/bin/gh`) which is the standard method on Debian/Ubuntu.

2. **Pip tools (crawl4ai, dspy, beads-viewer)**: Update commands use bare `pip install --upgrade <pkg>` (lines 106-108). On Ubuntu 24.04+ (and Fedora 38+, modern Debian), PEP 668 blocks bare pip installs with "externally managed environment" error. The auto-updater reports "Failed" with no workaround.

Related: #415 fixed PEP 668 in `setup.sh` but `tool-version-check.sh` was not updated.

## Expected Behavior

- Brew tools: detect the system package manager and use the appropriate update command (`apt-get install --only-upgrade` on Debian/Ubuntu, `dnf upgrade` on Fedora, `brew upgrade` on macOS)
- Pip tools: use `pipx upgrade` for Python CLI tools (already used for analytics-mcp at line 109), or `pip install --user --upgrade` as fallback

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ubuntu 24.04 with gh installed via apt (standard method)
2. Run `tool-version-check.sh --update`
3. Observe: gh version mismatch detected correctly, `brew upgrade gh` fails silently
4. Observe: crawl4ai update fails with PEP 668 error

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.283
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release
- **gh CLI**: 2.88.1 (installed via apt, `/usr/bin/gh`)
- **Python**: 3.12.3 (system, externally managed per PEP 668)
- **brew**: not installed

## Additional Context

The version detection side works correctly cross-platform — gh falls back to the GitHub API, pip tools use `pip show`. Only the update commands are platform-specific and currently macOS-only.

The analytics-mcp entry already uses `pipx upgrade` (line 109) and outscraper-mcp uses `uv tool upgrade` (line 110) — so the pattern for Python CLI tools exists, it's just not applied consistently.

title: discussion: tool-version-check.sh lists library dependencies alongside CLI tools
body:
## Description

`tool-version-check.sh` PIP_TOOLS includes both Python CLI tools and Python library dependencies in the same list:

- **CLI tools** (correct to track): `beads-viewer`, `analytics-mcp`, `outscraper-mcp-server` — these provide commands you run from the terminal
- **Library dependencies** (questionable): `crawl4ai`, `dspy` — these are imported by project code, not run from the CLI

The distinction matters because library dependencies are managed by project-level `pyproject.toml` / `requirements.txt` and installed in project venvs. The global copy that tool-version-check monitors and updates is not what projects actually use at runtime.

This creates a practical problem: the auto-updater installs library packages into the user-local Python scope (`~/.local/`), creating redundant copies that diverge from the pinned versions in project venvs. In one case, this accumulated 99 redundant packages in `~/.local/` over time.

There's also an internal contradiction: the framework's own `requirements.txt` pins dspy with explicit security comments ("Update versions deliberately, not automatically" — referencing the LiteLLM supply chain incident), yet `tool-version-check.sh` tries to auto-update dspy globally via bare pip.

## Options for consideration

### Option A: Remove library entries entirely

Remove `crawl4ai` and `dspy` from `PIP_TOOLS`. Library dependencies are the project's responsibility, managed by `pyproject.toml` in project venvs.

**Upside**: Clean separation of concerns. No more redundant global installs. No contradiction with pinned requirements.txt. Simplest change.

**Downside**: Users lose visibility into whether newer versions of key libraries exist. They'd need to check manually or use tools like dependabot/renovate on their projects.

### Option B: Track but don't update

Keep the entries for version awareness but move them to an "info-only" category that reports available updates without auto-installing. Something like: "crawl4ai: 0.8.6 in project venv, 0.9.0 available — update via your project venv."

**Upside**: Visibility into available updates without the side effects of global installation.

**Downside**: More complexity in the tool checker (new category). Risk of confusion — users may wonder why these aren't auto-updated like everything else. The checker would need venv discovery to report "installed in project venv" accurately.

### Option C: Move to project-level dependency checking

Remove from `tool-version-check.sh` (global tool scope) and create a separate project dependency health check that operates within project venvs.

**Upside**: Right tool for the job — checks deps where they actually live.

**Downside**: Larger scope of work. May overlap with existing tools (dependabot, renovate, `pip list --outdated`).

## My assessment

Option A seems most aligned with the framework's existing architecture — `requirements.txt` already treats these as deliberately pinned project deps, not auto-updated global tools. But the framework devs know the broader user base and may have reasons to prefer B or C.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.283
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS

title: discussion: add lightweight venv health checks for managed projects
body:
## Description

The framework has no awareness of Python virtual environments in managed projects. During a routine audit, we found:

- A broken editable install in a project venv (`.pth` file pointing to a deleted git worktree — `import deep_research` failed silently)
- 99 redundant packages in user-local `~/.local/` duplicating what was already in project venvs
- A root-level `.venv/` with no `requirements.txt` (undeclared, unreproducible dependencies)
- Stale documentation referencing a deleted venv path

None of these were caught proactively. The broken editable install would have been caught by a single `pip check` command.

## The question

Should the framework provide any level of Python venv awareness? There's a spectrum of options from "do nothing" to "full dependency management."

## Options for consideration

### Option A: Out of scope — do nothing

Venv management is language-specific. The framework is language-agnostic (manages repos, tasks, git, PRs). Adding Python venv support sets a precedent — should it also manage `node_modules`, Cargo deps, Go modules? Each language has its own packaging story.

**Upside**: No added complexity. Projects manage their own deps via their own tools (pip, poetry, uv, dependabot). Clear scope boundary.

**Downside**: Real problems (like broken editable installs) go undetected until someone manually checks. The framework already crossed the language-specific line with `tool-version-check.sh` tracking pip packages.

### Option B: Lightweight smoke test

Add a minimal venv health scan that discovers `.venv/` directories in managed repos and runs `pip check` (detects broken dependency requirements). Optionally flag stale editable installs (`.pth` files pointing to nonexistent paths). Report in the health dashboard alongside existing checks.

**Upside**: Catches real breakage (like the dead editable install) with minimal effort. `pip check` is a single command that catches dependency conflicts and missing packages. No version management, no update logic — just "is this venv broken?"

**Downside**: Python-specific addition to a language-agnostic framework. Requires discovering venvs (heuristic: look for `.venv/pyvenv.cfg` in project roots). May surface noise in projects with intentionally loose dependency specs.

### Option C: Full dependency health

Beyond smoke tests, report outdated packages within venvs, suggest updates, integrate with project-level dependency files. Essentially a framework-managed `pip list --outdated` scoped to project venvs.

**Upside**: Complete visibility into dependency health across all managed projects.

**Downside**: Significant scope. Overlaps with existing tools (dependabot, renovate, `pip-audit`). Blurs the line between framework responsibility and project responsibility. The framework would need to understand `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`, and `setup.cfg` — different projects use different approaches.

## My assessment

Option B (lightweight smoke test) seems proportional — it catches real breakage without trying to become a package manager. But Option A (do nothing) is also valid if the framework wants to maintain strict language-agnosticism. The devs know the framework's architectural intent better than I do.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.283
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS

title: discussion: Python packaging guidance for workers in worktree-based workflow
body:
## Description

The framework has no Python packaging guidance for workers. This caused a chain of real problems in a managed private repo with autonomous worker-driven development (a Python-heavy project with crawl4ai, multiple adapters, and a multi-phase plan):

1. **Broken editable install**: A worker ran `pip install -e .` from inside a git worktree, targeting the canonical repo's `.venv/`. The `.pth` file got the worktree's absolute path. When the worktree was removed after PR merge, importing the project's own package broke silently.
2. **99 redundant user-local packages**: Multiple workers ran `pip install` without an active venv. Packages accumulated in `~/.local/lib/python3.12/` — a duplicate of what was already in the project venv.
3. **Undeclared venv**: A worker created a `.venv/` and installed packages but never created a `requirements.txt`. The venv was unreproducible.
4. **Stale references**: A venv migration task updated the code but didn't catch all documentation references to the old path.

All four were found during a manual audit, not proactively caught.

## Root cause: the editable install + worktree interaction

This is the most interesting failure because it's specific to the framework's worktree workflow.

**Exact mechanism (traced from actual PR and task history):**

1. An earlier task created `shared/project/.venv/` in the canonical repo with a working editable install
2. A later task ("verify pip install works") was dispatched to a worker
3. Worker created a worktree for the task
4. The worktree had all git-tracked files but **no `.venv/`** — venvs are gitignored, they don't transfer between worktrees
5. Worker needed to verify the package installed. It found "the existing `.venv`" — the canonical repo's venv was the only one available
6. Worker ran `pip install -e shared/project/` from the worktree, using the canonical venv's pip
7. pip wrote the worktree's absolute path into the `.pth` file inside the canonical venv
8. PR merged, worktree removed. The `.pth` now pointed to a nonexistent directory
9. Importing the project's package failed silently in the canonical venv

The same pattern repeated with a subsequent task, except that worker had no venv activated at all — `pip install -e` went to `~/.local/`, creating 60+ transitive dependencies in user-local scope.

**The worker's PR body explicitly said**: "installs cleanly using the existing .venv" — the worker understood venvs and was trying to do the right thing. It just didn't know that editable installs create absolute path references that break when worktrees are removed.

## Why the workers made these decisions

Every level of guidance was silent on Python packaging:

| Source | Python packaging guidance |
|--------|--------------------------|
| Framework coding standards (`code-standards.md`) | None |
| Framework worktree docs (`git-workflow.md`, `pre-edit.md`) | No mention of non-git artifacts that don't transfer between worktrees |
| Framework build agent docs (`build-agent.md`) | None |
| Project plan (in `PLANS.md`) | No "Development Environment" section |
| Task briefs | No venv setup instructions |

Each worker independently solved "I need these packages available" with the most direct path. Locally reasonable decisions that created downstream problems.

## Context: autonomous workers

This is particularly important for users running most development through autonomous workers (via `/runners`, `/pulse`, `/full-loop`). The user isn't present to enforce packaging standards — the workers need to discover the right approach from the guidance available to them.

Workers already read: (1) framework AGENTS.md, (2) project AGENTS.md, (3) task briefs, (4) plan docs. Guidance placed in any of these would be discovered.

## Two levels of guidance to consider

### Framework level (applies to all workers, all repos)

Workers using worktrees need to know:

- **Worktrees don't include gitignored artifacts** (`.venv/`, `node_modules/`, build dirs). Workers must either create their own in the worktree or understand that the canonical repo's artifacts shouldn't be modified from a worktree context.
- **Never install Python packages to user-local or system scope.** If a project has a `.venv/`, use it (from the correct path). If it has `pyproject.toml` but no `.venv/`, create one.
- **Editable installs (`pip install -e`) create absolute path references.** In a worktree, that path becomes invalid after worktree removal. Workers doing editable installs in worktrees should create a throwaway venv inside the worktree, not modify the canonical repo's venv.

This is framework-level because worktrees are a framework concept, and Python is common enough across projects that workers will encounter this regularly.

### Plan/project level (project's responsibility, but framework could recommend)

Individual Python projects need a "Development Environment" section in their plan or AGENTS.md covering:
- Which venv(s) exist and where
- How to create/recreate them (`python3 -m venv .venv && pip install -e ".[dev]"`)
- How to run tests (`source .venv/bin/activate && pytest`)
- What not to do (install globally, modify canonical venv from worktrees)

The framework can't write this for every project, but it could recommend the pattern — similar to how it recommends task brief structure via templates.

## Options for consideration

### Option A: Minimal — add a paragraph to worktree docs

Add a note to `git-workflow.md` or `pre-edit.md` about non-git artifacts and the editable install interaction. Workers would see this because worktree docs are referenced during the pre-edit flow.

**Upside**: Smallest change, directly addresses the root cause.
**Downside**: Easy to miss in a long doc. Doesn't address the broader "where to install" question.

### Option B: Add Python packaging section to coding standards

Add a "Python Projects" section to `code-standards.md` covering venv usage, where to install, editable install caveats in worktrees, and requirements file discipline.

**Upside**: Workers read coding standards for every code task. Comprehensive. Covers both the worktree interaction and the general "don't install globally" problem.
**Downside**: Language-specific addition to potentially language-agnostic standards. Sets precedent for Node.js, Rust, Go sections.

### Option C: Plan template addition

Add a "Development Environment" section to the plan template (or a plan template) that prompts plan authors to document their Python setup.

**Upside**: Ensures project-specific guidance exists. Works for any language, not just Python.
**Downside**: Only helps future plans. Doesn't address the framework-level worktree interaction.

### Option D: Combination (B + C)

Framework coding standards cover the universal rules (worktree interaction, don't install globally). Plan template covers project-specific setup. Belt and suspenders.

**Upside**: Covers both levels. Workers get framework rules automatically and project-specific instructions when they read the plan.
**Downside**: More to maintain. Two places to keep consistent.

## Related issues

- #6762 — `tool-version-check.sh` platform bugs (brew + PEP 668)
- #6763 — library deps listed as global tools in tool checker
- #6764 — lightweight venv health checks for managed projects

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.283
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release

## Agent doc simplification (automated scan)

**File:** `.agents/tools/marketing/cro/CHAPTER-10.md`
**Detected topic:** Checkout Flow Optimization - Deep Dive
**Current size:** 538 lines (threshold: 500)

### Classify before acting

**First, determine the file type** — the correct action depends on whether this is an instruction doc or a reference corpus:

- **Instruction doc** (agent rules, workflows, decision trees, operational procedures): Tighten prose, reorder by importance, split if multiple concerns. Follow guidance below.
- **Reference corpus** (SKILL.md, domain knowledge base, textbook-style content with self-contained sections): Do NOT compress content. Instead, split into chapter files with a slim index. See `tools/code-review/code-simplifier.md` "Reference corpora" classification (GH#6432).

### For instruction docs — proposed action

Tighten and restructure this agent doc. Follow `tools/build-agent/build-agent.md` guidance. Key principles:

1. **Preserve all institutional knowledge** — every verbose rule exists because something broke without it. Do not remove task IDs, incident references, error statistics, or decision rationale. Compress prose, not knowledge.
2. **Order by importance** — most critical instructions first (primacy effect: LLMs weight earlier context more heavily). Security rules, core workflow, then edge cases.
3. **Split if needed** — if the file covers multiple distinct concerns, extract sub-docs with a parent index. Use progressive disclosure (pointers, not inline content).
4. **Use search patterns, not line numbers** — any `file:line_number` references to other files go stale on every edit. Use `rg "pattern"` or section heading references instead.

### For reference corpora — proposed action

1. **Extract each major section** into its own file (e.g., `01-introduction.md`, `02-fundamentals.md`)
2. **Replace the original with a slim index** (~100-200 lines) — table of contents with one-line descriptions and file pointers
3. **Zero content loss** — every line moves to a chapter file, nothing is deleted or compressed
4. **Reconcile existing chapter files** — if partial splits already exist, deduplicate and keep the most complete version

### Verification

- Content preservation: all code blocks, URLs, task ID references (`tNNN`, `GH#NNN`), and command examples must be present before and after
- No broken internal links or references
- Agent behaviour unchanged (test with a representative query if possible)
- For reference corpora: `wc -l` total of chapter files >= original line count minus index overhead

### Confidence: medium

Automated scan identified this file by size. The best simplification strategy requires human judgment — some large files are appropriately large. Reference corpora (SKILL.md, domain knowledge bases) need restructuring into chapters, not content reduction.

title: bug: Framework Validation / Complexity Analysis fails on PRs due to pre-existing violations in unrelated files
body:
## Problem

The Complexity Analysis check in Framework Validation fails on PRs that don't touch any complex files. This blocks clean PRs from merging.

## Evidence

- PR #6861 (only modifies `.agents/tools/deployment/daytona.md`) fails Framework Validation
- The failures are in pre-existing files: `101domains-helper.sh` (nesting 16), `accessibility-audit-helper.sh` (nesting 10), `add-skill-helper.sh` (nesting 56), etc.
- These violations exist on main and are not introduced by the PR

## Root Cause

The Complexity Analysis check runs against ALL files in the repo, not just the PR diff. Pre-existing violations in unrelated files cause the check to fail on every PR.

## Fix Options

1. Change the check to only analyze files changed in the PR diff
2. Establish a baseline and only fail on regressions (new violations)
3. Fix the pre-existing violations in the blocking files

Option 2 (regression-only) is the most pragmatic — it unblocks current PRs while still catching new violations.

title: json_set_nested skips existing MCP entries, preventing stale config updates
body:
## Problem

`json_set_nested()` in `.agents/scripts/ai-cli-config.sh:50` skips if the key already exists:

```python
if inner_key in config[outer_key]:
    print(f"{inner_key} already configured in {file_path} - skipping")
```

This means when MCP package names change (e.g., `@anthropic-ai/mcp-server-playwright` → `@playwright/mcp`) or transport changes (local → remote), `setup.sh` / `aidevops update` cannot fix the stale entries. Users are stuck with broken configs until they manually edit the JSON.

## Impact

Discovered in t1685/GH#6870 — 3 MCPs showed "Connection closed" errors in OpenCode because the deployed config had stale entries that setup couldn't update.

## Proposed Fix

Add an `--update` / force mode to `json_set_nested` that overwrites existing entries. The MCP registration functions should use this mode for entries where the source of truth is the generator script (not user customization).

Alternatively, add a version/hash field to MCP entries so the adapter can detect when the generator's definition has changed and needs to overwrite.

## Files

- `.agents/scripts/ai-cli-config.sh:22` — `json_set_nested()`
- `.agents/scripts/mcp-config-adapter.sh` — all `_register_mcp_*` functions call `json_set_nested`

title: t1686: feat: GitHub comment-based optimistic locking for cross-machine dispatch dedup
body:
**Task ID:** `t1686` | **Status:** in-progress | **Estimate:** `~2h`
**Logged:** 2026-03-27
**Tags:** `feature` `orchestration` `dedup`

## Problem

Multiple aidevops runners (different users/machines) dispatch workers for the same GitHub issue because the current dedup guards have a race window. The existing `is_assigned` check queries GitHub assignees before dispatch, but two runners can both read "unassigned" simultaneously, both assign themselves, and both dispatch — wasting compute on duplicate work.

Current mitigations (GH#4947):
- **Startup jitter** (0-30s random delay) — reduces collision probability but doesn't eliminate it
- **Local process dedup** — only sees same-machine processes
- **Dispatch ledger** — local JSONL file, no cross-user visibility
- **GitHub assignee check** — non-atomic read-then-write, race window remains

## Solution

Implement **GitHub comment-based optimistic locking**. Before dispatching, a runner posts a claim comment with a unique nonce on the issue. After a consensus window (5-10s), it re-reads comments. If its claim is the oldest within the window, it proceeds. If another runner's claim is older, it backs off.

This is optimistic locking via GitHub's append-only comment timeline — two runners can both post claims, but only one will be chronologically first.

### Protocol

1. Post claim comment: `<!-- DISPATCH_CLAIM nonce=UUID runner=LOGIN ts=ISO -->`
2. Sleep consensus window (configurable, default 8s)
3. Re-read issue comments from last 30s
4. Parse all `DISPATCH_CLAIM` comments
5. If this runner's claim is the oldest → proceed with dispatch
6. If another runner's claim is older → back off, delete own claim comment

### Design decisions

- **HTML comment format** — invisible in rendered issue timeline, no noise
- **Nonce-based** — prevents replay/confusion with stale claims
- **Consensus window** — configurable via `DISPATCH_CLAIM_WINDOW` env var
- **Claim cleanup** — losing claims are deleted; winning claims are deleted after dispatch completes
- **Fail-open** — API errors during claim → proceed (same as existing `is_assigned` behaviour)

## Files

- `.agents/scripts/dispatch-claim-helper.sh` — new helper implementing the claim protocol
- `.agents/scripts/dispatch-dedup-helper.sh` — integrate `claim` as a new subcommand
- `.agents/scripts/commands/pulse.md` — update dedup guard documentation
- `.agents/scripts/tests/test-dispatch-claim-helper.sh` — unit tests

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `dispatch-claim-helper.sh claim <issue> <slug>` posts HTML comment claim, waits, returns exit 0 (won) or exit 1 (lost)
- [ ] `dispatch-claim-helper.sh release <issue> <slug>` cleans up claim comments
- [ ] Losing runner backs off without dispatching
- [ ] API failures fail-open (proceed with dispatch)
- [ ] Claim comments are invisible in rendered GitHub issue view (HTML comments)
- [ ] Consensus window is configurable via env var
- [ ] ShellCheck clean
- [ ] Tests pass

title: bug: invalid x-api-key error when OAuth access token expires — silent refresh failure
body:
## Description

When the OAuth access token expires, the system sends the expired token and Anthropic returns "invalid x-api-key" instead of triggering a proper refresh. The user must manually re-add the account to force a fresh OAuth flow.

## Expected Behavior

When an OAuth access token expires, the system should:
1. Detect the 401/invalid token response
2. Use the refresh token to obtain a new access token
3. Retry the request with the new token — all silently

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Add an Anthropic account to the OAuth pool via `oauth-pool-helper.sh add anthropic`
2. Wait for the access token to expire (or force expiry)
3. Make an API call that uses the token
4. Observe "invalid x-api-key" error instead of auto-refresh

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.1.319 (latest)
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: MINGW64_NT-10.0-19045 (Git Bash on Windows)
- **gh CLI**: 2.88.1
- **OAuth pool**: 1 account (jpham4567@gmail.com)

## Additional Context

- This is distinct from "API key missing" — a token IS being sent but is invalid/expired
- Related: #5607 (scheduled token refresh) was recently completed but may not cover all failure modes
- The fix in #5586 implemented refresh token exchange but silent failures may still occur
